Problem Statement
Problem: Algorithms - 29
Prove the NP-Hardness of the following decision problem: Given an undirected graph G,
determine whether there exists a simple path in G that visits exactly |V (G)|−17 vertices.

0001 | Solution:
0002 | Solution. **Claim:** The decision problem
0003 | LongPath17 : “Given an undirected graph G = (V, E), does there exist a simple path that visits exactly
0004 | is NP-hard. (In fact, it is NP-complete, since it is clearly in NP: a certificate is a list of
0005 | vertices forming the path, which can be verified in polynomial time.)
0006 | **Proof (by reduction from Hamiltonian Path):** Recall that a **Hamiltonian path** in
0007 | a graph is a simple path that visits every vertex exactly once. The Hamiltonian Path decision
0008 | problem (given a graph H, does H have a Hamiltonian path?) is a classical NP-complete
0009 | problem (see, e.g., Garey–Johnson 1979 or Karp 1972). We will show a polynomial-time
0010 | reduction from Hamiltonian Path to LongPath17.
0011 | Given an arbitrary instance H = (VH, EH) of Hamiltonian Path (where |VH| = n), we
0012 | construct an instance G = (VG, EG) for LongPath17 as follows:
0013 | - Start with G being a copy of H. Thus initially VG = VH and EG = EH. - Add 17
0014 | new **isolated** vertices to G (that is, 17 vertices with no edges incident to them). Let
0015 | U = {u1, u2, . . . , u17} denote these new vertices. - Define VG := VH ∪U. Keep EG := EH
0016 | (no new edges are added, so the ui’s remain isolated).
0017 | This construction clearly takes polynomial time (in fact, it is just O(n) time to add 17
0018 | new vertices). Now G has |VG| = |VH| + 17 = n + 17 vertices. We claim that H has a
0019 | Hamiltonian path if and only if G has a simple path visiting exactly |VG| −17 vertices.
0020 | “⇒” **(If H has a Hamiltonian path, then G has a path through |VG| −17 vertices):**
0021 | Suppose H has a Hamiltonian path PH that visits all n = |VH| vertices of H. Consider the
0022 | same sequence of vertices PH viewed as a path in G. Since G contains all the vertices and
0023 | edges of H, PH is also a valid path in G (it uses only edges from EH ⊆EG). This path PH in
0024 | G visits all n of the original vertices VH. Importantly, it does not visit any of the 17 isolated
0025 | vertices U, because there are no edges connecting U to the rest of the graph (so an isolated
0026 | vertex cannot be reached without leaving the path). Thus, PH is a simple path in G that
0027 | visits exactly n vertices. But |VG| = n+17, so PH visits exactly (n+17)−17 = n = |VG|−17
0028 | vertices of G, as required. Therefore, G has a simple path visiting |VG| −17 vertices.
0029 | “⇐” **(If G has a path through |VG| −17 vertices, then H has a Hamiltonian path):**
0030 | Now assume G has a simple path PG that visits exactly |VG| −17 vertices. We will show H
0031 | must have a Hamiltonian path. Since |VG| = n+17, the path PG visits exactly (n+17)−17 =
0032 | n vertices. In other words, PG visits n distinct vertices of G. There are only n original
0033 | vertices in VH, so any set of n distinct vertices of G must include all the original vertices
0034 | VH (and possibly some of the added ones). However, note that it is **impossible** for PG
0035 | to include any of the isolated vertices ui ∈U as part of a single connected path through n
0036 | vertices. Each ui has no edges to any other vertex, so a path in G that includes an isolated ui
0037 | cannot continue on to any other vertex — it would be “stuck” at ui. The only possible path
0038 | containing an isolated vertex would be a trivial path of length 0 (just the isolated vertex
0039 | itself), which clearly cannot cover n vertices. Therefore, PG cannot visit any of the isolated
0040 | vertices. (More formally: since PG visits n > 1 vertices and is a single connected path, it
0041 | must lie entirely in the connected component of G that contains H; any isolated vertex is in
0042 | its own separate component and cannot be part of a multi-vertex path.)
0043 | 1
0044 | 
0045 | Thus PG must visit n vertices all drawn from VH. But |VH| = n, so PG actually visits
0046 | every vertex of H. In other words, PG (when restricted to the vertex set VH and edges EH)
0047 | is a Hamiltonian path of the graph H. (Since PG uses only edges from EG, and edges in EG
0048 | connecting vertices in VH are exactly EH, the restriction of PG to H is indeed a path in H
0049 | that goes through every vertex of H exactly once.) Hence H has a Hamiltonian path.
0050 | We have shown that H has a Hamiltonian path if and only if G has a simple path
0051 | visiting |VG| −17 vertices. Because the transformation from H to G was clearly computable
0052 | in polynomial time, this is a valid polynomial-time reduction. Since Hamiltonian Path is NP-
0053 | hard, it follows that our LongPath17 decision problem is NP-hard as well. (As mentioned,
0054 | it is also in NP, so it is NP-complete.) This completes the proof.
